item.text: {"text":"Closest prior art: Petrov and Macdonald’s RecSys 2022 paper, [Effective and Efficient Training for Sequential Recommendation using Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643), with [official implementation](https://github.com/asash/bert4rec_repro). RSS draws c=max(1,floor(nτ)) target positions **with replacement**, using per-draw probabilities pᵢ=f(i)/Σⱼf(j), typically exponential recency importance. Algorithm 1 removes selected positions, compacts the remaining input, and constructs a set of positive item IDs; repeated draws do not multiply a target’s contribution. Unselected interactions later than an early target remain available as context. Thus RSS differs from prefix-only next-item training and position-preserving BERT4Rec masking. The original experiments apply RSS to GRU4Rec, Caser and SASRec; BERT4Rec is a comparison baseline, not an evaluated RSS adaptation. [Original paper, Algorithm 1 and conclusion](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643v2).\n\nKey mathematical distinction, derived from that sampling procedure: a position’s actual inclusion probability is qᵢ=1−(1−pᵢ)^c, not pᵢ or cpᵢ. Expected distinct target positions equal Σᵢqᵢ and can be substantially fewer than c. For repeated item IDs, item-level inclusion becomes 1−(1−Σᵢ:itemᵢ=v pᵢ)^c. Recency therefore changes target exposure through inclusion probabilities; it does not automatically impose explicit recency loss weights. Drawing targets without replacement, retaining duplicate multiplicities, or additionally weighting losses by pᵢ defines different objectives. RSS supports multiple-positive losses and compares BCE with LambdaRank; its recency sampling and ranking-loss effects should be distinguished. [Sampling and loss definitions](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643v2)."}
